design_detail: Registered report (Stage 1 in-principle acceptance 25 January 2022 through Peer Community In Registered Reports; materials, code and data on OSF) of an online randomized between-participants vignette experiment, 2 × 2 × 2: health condition ('drug use' vs 'health concern'), label ('chronically relapsing brain disease' vs 'problem') and attributional judgment (high treatment stability: in a treatment programme and committed to success, vs low: has visited a doctor and the condition could get worse or improve). 1,613 adults read one vignette about 'Alex' for at least 60 s, then completed the Stigma and Attribution Assessment (five subscales), the Personal and Perceived Public Stigma Measure (total) in random order, and a Financial Discrimination Task (rewards and punishments of 0 to 100 pence given to Alex's answers on a sham learning platform). Each research question was tested with Welch t-tests plus equivalence tests (two one-sided tests, bounds d ±0.20, α=.01); questions 2 and 3 were analysed within the drug-use arm only. Designed to explain why Kelly et al. (2021) and Rundle et al. (2021) disagreed about the brain-disease label.
can_establish: That in this online sample of adults who said they had no substance use or psychiatric diagnosis and knew of none in a close relative, describing a person's difficulty as drug use rather than a health concern caused large or nearly large increases in self-reported social distance, perceived danger and public stigma (d 0.78 to 0.95), and that calling the drug use a 'chronically relapsing brain disease' rather than a 'problem' caused stronger agreement that it was genetic or disease-based, after a single short vignette.
cannot_establish: How people who use drugs are actually treated by the public, clinicians or services (one hypothetical allocation task, no real behaviour); how people with a substance use or psychiatric diagnosis, or a close relative with one, respond (they were not eligible); or whether the label or the treatment framing has small effects on social distance, danger, optimism or public stigma, which the study could not tell apart from zero or from trivial (inconclusive results).

sample.recruitment: Online volunteers recruited through university research-participation schemes (SONA), Prolific and social media (Twitter, LinkedIn), paid in course credit or £5.00 per hour; country of residence not stated in the article (Method › Design and Participants, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18 or over and confirming that they did not have, and did not know a close relative with, a past or current substance use or psychiatric diagnosis. Excluded after recruitment: 9 of 1,622 (6 failed attention checks, 2 withdrew data, 1 implausible response time); for each research question, people who failed that question's manipulation check: 53 (3.29%) for RQ1, 32 (3.78%) for RQ2, 102 (11.96%) for RQ3 (Method › Design and Participants, 3rd paragraph; Results).
sample.demographics: Largest age band 18–25 years (36.5%); 55.9% women; 77.1% White; fuller demographics only in a supplement (File S2), not read.
sample.attrition: Single session; 0.6% excluded overall; manipulation-check exclusions per research question as above, not broken down by condition.
sample.selection_effects: A convenience sample of students and online panel members, mostly young, that deliberately excludes people with a substance use or psychiatric diagnosis in themselves or a close relative (people who used drugs without such a diagnosis were not excluded by this criterion); vignette judgments by such a sample may differ from those of clinicians, employers or the wider public.

exposure.measurement: Randomized vignette condition (assigned by the Inquisit software). The vignette (an image in the article, read on screen): Alex has serious trouble at home and work because of increasing drug use, or a health concern; is now in a treatment programme, or has visited a doctor; learns from staff that the condition is best understood as a chronically relapsing brain disease, or as a problem; and is committed to doing all they can to succeed after treatment, or is told the condition could get worse but could improve with treatment.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable (vignette experiment). No drug is named in the vignette.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable. The authors chose not to vary the substance (footnote 1); four questionnaire items in the drug-use arm refer to opioid addiction.

comparison.controls: The other level of each factor: health concern vs drug use (RQ1, all participants); 'problem' vs 'chronically relapsing brain disease' (RQ2, drug-use arm); high vs low treatment stability (RQ3, drug-use arm).
comparison.matching: Randomization; balance of characteristics across conditions is not reported in the article.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Participants' prior beliefs about addiction and contact with people who use drugs were not measured as moderators.

outcomes.instruments: Stigma and Attribution Assessment (Kelly et al., 2021; 22 items, 1–6 agreement; subscales social distance, perceived danger, prognostic optimism, blame attribution, need for continued care; α in this sample printed as .88, .79, .70 and .69, four values for five subscales, so which subscale lacks one is unclear); Personal and Perceived Public Stigma Measure (Rundle et al., 2021; 23 items, 1–4; total score, subscale α .70 to .91); Financial Discrimination Task (Jones et al., 2022): rewards for Alex's three correct and punishments for three incorrect answers, 0 to 300 pence each (Measures).
outcomes.validity_norms: Scoring direction differs by subscale: higher scores mean more danger and more need for continued care, but less social distance, more blame and more prognostic optimism (Measures; Table 1 note). The three blame items attribute the condition to the disease process (for example that Alex's opioid addiction is genetic in origin), so a higher blame score means stronger agreement with a genetic or disease cause (Discussion, 3rd paragraph). The financial task is a hypothetical, indirect measure of discrimination.
outcomes.operationalization: Stigma as self-reported attitudes on the subscales and total; discrimination as lower rewards and larger punishments in the task. Each difference classified as meaningful (significant at α=.01 and interval outside d ±0.20), equivalent (not significant and interval inside ±0.20) or inconclusive.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Conservative α of .01 for 8 outcomes × 3 research questions; no further correction.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Self-completed online measures; participants knew the vignette they had read but not the comparison; the hypotheses were non-directional.

analysis.effect_sizes: Cohen's d with intervals labelled 99% CI (Results; see reporting issues). RQ1, drug use vs health concern: social distance d=.87 [.74, .99], perceived danger .78 [.66, .90], public stigma .95 [.82, 1.07], blame −.35 [−.47, −.23] (all meaningful); prognostic optimism −.06 [−.18, .06] (equivalent); continued care .09 [−.03, .21] (inconclusive); reward −.03 [−.14, .09] (equivalent); punishment .14 [.02, .26] (inconclusive). RQ2, brain disease vs problem: blame .54 [.38, .71] (meaningful); continued care .01 (equivalent); social distance −.20 [−.36, −.03], prognostic optimism −.07, danger −.11, public stigma −.18 [−.34, −.02], reward .15 (inconclusive); punishment .007 (equivalent). RQ3, low vs high stability: social distance −.23, danger .19, blame −.11, prognostic optimism −.17 [−.35, −.004], continued care .11, public stigma .31 [.14, .48], reward −.13 (all inconclusive); punishment −.02 (equivalent). Table 1 (an image, read on screen) gives means and SDs: for example public stigma 50.59 (8.86) vs 42.15 (8.99) in RQ1 and 49.62 (8.89) vs 51.20 (8.78) in RQ2; blame 8.61 (2.63) vs 7.22 (2.51) in RQ2; punishment 62.05 (59.59) vs 53.96 (54.18) pence in RQ1. Editors' check: the RQ2 d values recomputed from Table 1's means and SDs match the text (blame 0.54, public stigma −0.18, social distance 0.20 in magnitude).
analysis.covariates: None (two-group comparisons per research question; interactions between factors not tested).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Stage 1 protocol accepted in principle on 25 January 2022 (PCI RR, https://osf.io/4vscg); all manipulations, measures and exclusions said to be reported; PCI RR bias-control Level 6. The Stage 1 protocol and supplements (Table S1, Files S2 and S3) were not read, so deviations could not be checked; restricting RQ2 and RQ3 to the drug-use arm is stated in the Results without saying whether it was planned.
analysis.selective_reporting: All research questions and all eight outcomes are reported for each, including null and inconclusive results; exploratory analyses with wider equivalence bounds are only in File S3.
analysis.power: Planned 1,578 participants for 90% power to detect equivalence within d ±0.20 at α=.01 (2,804 would have been needed for ±0.15, beyond the funding). Because RQ2 and RQ3 used only the drug-use arm, the smallest cells (392 and 362) allowed equivalence bounds of only ±0.28 and ±0.30 (Method › Design and Participants, 2nd–3rd paragraphs).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Large effects of calling the person's difficulty drug use rather than a health concern on self-reported social distance, danger and public stigma (d about 0.8 to 0.95) and a smaller effect on the blame subscale (d −0.35); the brain-disease label raised agreement that the condition is genetic or disease-based (d 0.54), with small, inconclusive differences on the other measures, social distance and public stigma being slightly lower with the label (printed intervals −0.36 to −0.03 and −0.34 to −0.02, which do not include zero; at 99% the public-stigma interval would reach zero); in the financial task, slightly larger punishments with the drug-use description (d 0.14, 0.02 to 0.26; p = .005), which the study's rule classes as inconclusive, and otherwise equivalent or inconclusive differences; the treatment-stability framing was inconclusive on every self-report measure and on rewards, and equivalent on punishments.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports "Greater (genetic) blame" with the brain-disease label. The blame items state that the condition is genetic or disease-caused, and the authors' own Discussion reads the label as possibly absolving personal blame by shifting it to brain pathology (Discussion, 3rd paragraph); a reader of the abstract alone could take the result to mean more stigmatizing blame. Whether the contrast drawn with Kelly et al. (2021), who reported lower blame with this label, reflects a real difference or the scoring direction of the same subscale is not settled in the paper. The conclusion that labels affect discrete elements of stigma rests mainly on the health-condition contrast, in which the questionnaire wording also differed (items naming opioid addiction in the drug-use arm only). The suggestion that attitudes do not translate reliably into discrimination rests on one hypothetical financial task with equivalent or inconclusive results and passes over the RQ1 punishment difference, which was significant at the study's α (p = .005) though classed as inconclusive; the proposal that addiction is a functional attribution was not tested. The authors label inconclusive results as such.

timeline.event: Randomized study of two commonly used terms for people with substance-related conditions (Kelly & Westerhoff, 2010), on the label side of the same question; not yet appraised

Kelly et al. (2021), 3,635 participants, opioid-dependence vignettes with six labels: 'chronically relapsing brain disease' went with lower blame but lower prognostic optimism and higher danger and need for continued care (as described in this paper).
Rundle et al. (2021), 872 participants: public stigma highest for alcohol use disorder; endorsement of a disease model not associated with public stigma (as described in this paper).
This registered report: large stigma effects of naming drug use, greater genetic or disease attribution with the brain-disease label, other label effects inconclusive.

replication.where_it_stands: Two of the three large vignette studies (Rundle et al., 2021, and this one) compared a described drug or alcohol problem with other health conditions and found that it drew more self-reported stigma; Kelly et al. (2021) had no comparison condition, although these authors count it as agreeing (Introduction, 6th paragraph; Discussion, 6th paragraph). The three disagree on what the brain-disease label does to blame, danger and optimism, partly because they used different measures and vignettes. None measured real-world treatment of people who use drugs.

funding.funder: Internal funding from Aston University awarded to C.R. Pennington, R.L. Monk, D. Heim, A.K. Rose, T. Gough, G. Knibb and A. Jones; open-access funding from the School of Psychology, Aston University (Acknowledgements; article notes).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors have no known conflicts of interest to declare (Acknowledgements).
funding.affiliations_note: Aston University; Edge Hill University; Liverpool Centre for Alcohol Research; Liverpool John Moores University; University of Liverpool; Liverpool Hope University (Author Affiliations). The Financial Discrimination Task was developed by members of the team (Jones et al., 2022). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A pre-registered experiment, powered for differences of about d 0.15 in each comparison, that crosses the labels with the full factorial and samples clinicians, employers and members of the public as well as people with lived experience, uses wording-matched questionnaires and a blame measure that separates personal blame from biological attribution, and adds real decisions (for example referrals or allocation of actual resources) with follow-up.

domains.note: Assignment by the Inquisit software to eight conditions; concealment inherent in online assignment; balance of characteristics across conditions is in a supplement not read.

People who failed the manipulation check for a question were excluded from that analysis (3.3% to 12%), a per-protocol analysis; numbers by condition are not given, and the treatment-stability check asked about the setting (treatment programme or doctor) rather than perceived stability.

Self-reported attitudes after an explicit vignette, open to demand effects; questionnaire wording differed between the drug-use and health-concern arms (opioid addiction named in four items in one arm); the blame subscale measures genetic or disease attribution, so its label invites misreading; internal consistency .69 to .91.
Registered report with all outcomes reported; provisional, because the Stage 1 protocol was not compared here, and the restriction of RQ2 and RQ3 to the drug-use arm is not stated as planned.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A well-conducted, pre-registered randomized experiment with transparent equivalence testing and reporting of null and inconclusive results. Concerns are the per-protocol exclusions on manipulation checks, the questionnaire wording that differed between arms for the health-condition comparison, and a blame subscale whose name does not match what it measures. It may be cited for the large effect of describing a condition as drug use (rather than a health concern) on self-reported social distance, danger and public stigma in a non-clinical online sample, and for the brain-disease label increasing genetic or disease attribution, described as such; it may not be cited for effects on real discrimination or on clinicians, or as showing that the brain-disease label increases or reduces stigma overall.

key_findings.finding: 1,613 adults (1,622 recruited; 9 excluded) from university research-participation schemes (SONA), Prolific and social media were randomized to one of eight vignette conditions; largest age band 18–25 years (36.5%), 55.9% women, 77.1% White; people with their own or a close relative's substance use or psychiatric diagnosis were not eligible.
key_findings.locator: Method › Design and Participants, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Procedure

key_findings.finding: Describing Alex's difficulty as drug use rather than a health concern (819 vs 741) produced greater self-reported social distance (d=.87, 99% CI as printed .74 to .99), perceived danger (d=.78, .66 to .90) and public stigma (d=.95, .82 to 1.07), and lower scores on the blame subscale (d=−.35, −.47 to −.23); prognostic optimism was equivalent (d=−.06) and continued care inconclusive (d=.09). Means: public stigma 50.59 vs 42.15; perceived danger 17.37 vs 13.32; social distance 18.84 vs 23.76 (lower = more distance).
key_findings.locator: Results › Research Question 1, 1st paragraph; Table 1, RQ1 columns
key_findings.note: Table 1 is an image, read on screen. The intervals labelled 99% match 98% intervals (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: In the financial task, describing the condition as drug use left rewards unchanged within the equivalence bounds (d=−.03, equivalent; 248.11 vs 249.72 pence) and went with slightly larger punishments (62.05 vs 53.96 pence; d=.14, .02 to .26; Table 1: Welch t(1557.96)=2.81, p=.005), a difference significant at the study's α of .01 but classed as inconclusive because its interval also overlaps the ±0.20 equivalence bounds.
key_findings.locator: Results › Research Question 1, 1st paragraph; Table 1, RQ1 Reward and Punishment rows
key_findings.note: Table 1 is an image: t and p as read on screen by the second reader; the first reader's means and SDs (62.05, 59.59; 53.96, 54.18) reproduce them (editors' recomputation).

key_findings.finding: Within the drug-use arm, the label 'chronically relapsing brain disease' rather than 'problem' (392 vs 423) raised blame-subscale scores, whose items attribute the condition to genetic or disease causes (d=.54, .38 to .71; means 8.61 vs 7.22); need for continued care was equivalent (d=.01); social distance (d=−.20, −.36 to −.03), prognostic optimism (−.07), danger (−.11) and public stigma (−.18, −.34 to −.02) were inconclusive; on the means, the brain-disease label went with slightly less social distance (19.46 vs 18.38, higher = less distance) and slightly lower public stigma (49.62 vs 51.20).
key_findings.locator: Results › Research Question 2, 1st paragraph; Table 1, RQ2 columns; Discussion, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The label did not reliably change the financial task: rewards inconclusive (d=.15), punishments equivalent (d=.007).

Within the drug-use arm, framing treatment as likely to succeed (high stability) or as an uncertain course (low stability) (383 vs 362) produced only inconclusive differences on every self-report measure (for example public stigma d=.31, .14 to .48, higher with low stability; social distance d=−.23) and on rewards; punishments were equivalent. 102 participants (11.96%) failed this manipulation check.
key_findings.locator: Results › Research Question 3, 1st paragraph; Table 1, RQ3 columns
key_findings.note: Besides the outlook, the two versions differ in setting: in the 'likely to succeed' (high-stability) version Alex is now in a treatment programme, in the 'uncertain' version Alex has visited a doctor, and the manipulation check asked about this setting (Method › Manipulation and Attention Checks; vignette image).

key_findings.finding: Power: 1,578 participants were planned for 90% power to show equivalence within d ±0.20 at α=.01 (2,804 for ±0.15 was beyond the funding); with RQ2 and RQ3 restricted to the drug-use arm, the detectable equivalence bounds were ±0.28 and ±0.30.

The authors conclude that problematic substance use is among the most stigmatized health conditions (agreeing with Kelly et al., 2021 and Rundle et al., 2021), that the brain-disease label's effects remain mixed, that aggregated and multidimensional stigma measures lead to different conclusions, and propose that addiction works as a functional attribution, used to assign or displace responsibility depending on context (a proposal, not tested here).
key_findings.note: 'Agreeing with Kelly et al., 2021' is the authors' reading: as the Introduction (4th and 6th paragraphs) describes them, only Rundle et al. (2021) compared an alcohol use disorder with other conditions, and Kelly et al. (2021) had no comparison health condition.

reporting_issues.issue: The intervals labelled 99% CI match 98% intervals: for example, for public stigma in RQ3 (d=.31, groups of 362 and 383) a 99% interval is about .12 to .50 and a 98% interval .14 to .48, the printed values; the same holds for all 24 printed intervals, 8 outcomes in each of the 3 research questions (editors' calculation from the Table 1 means, SDs and group sizes, normal approximation to the standard error of d; done independently by the second reader and the adjudicator). A 98% interval is what a two one-sided tests procedure at α=.01 produces.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML: Method › Analytic Strategy; Results, all three research questions
reporting_issues.consequence: The intervals are narrower than labelled; at 99% the RQ2 public-stigma interval would include zero. The meaningful/equivalent/inconclusive classifications reported do not change.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints p<.01 for the RQ2 public-stigma Welch test, t(806.59)=−2.55, which corresponds to p≈.011 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML: Table 1, RQ2 Public stigma row
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; consistent with the 99% interval including zero; the result is classified inconclusive in any case.

reporting_issues.issue: 102 manipulation-check failures for RQ3 are given as 11.96% of the drug-use arm, but that arm had 847 participants (392 + 423 + 32 from RQ2), so 102 is 12.0%; 11.96% implies 853.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML: Results › Research Questions 2 and 3

reporting_issues.issue: Signs and degrees of freedom are inconsistent in places: for social distance the sign of d in the text is opposite to the sign of t in Table 1 for RQ1 and RQ2, for RQ3 the t is positive although the low-stability mean is lower (18.14 vs 19.38); the RQ3 punishment t is printed as 0.21 although the low-stability mean is lower (62.21 vs 63.16) and d is −.02, so it should be −0.21; two RQ3 rows give different degrees of freedom for the two tests of the same comparison (742.93 and 742.82; 753.49 and 735.49).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the direction of each effect has to be read from the means, remembering that a lower social-distance score means more distance.

reporting_issues.issue: In the drug-use arm, four questionnaire items refer to Alex's opioid addiction (they were edited to remove the term for the health-concern arm), although the vignette itself mentions only drug use, not opioids or addiction.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML: Measures › Stigma and Attribution Assessment; vignette (image) under Vignette Development
reporting_issues.consequence: The RQ1 comparison varies the questionnaire wording as well as the vignette, which affects at least the blame subscale; the RQ2 and RQ3 comparisons, within one arm, are not affected.

reporting_issues.issue: Two descriptive slips: the text calls the 36.5% aged 18–25 'the majority' (it is the largest age group, not a majority), and it says all Stigma and Attribution Assessment subscales had acceptable internal reliability (above .70) in this sample, while one printed alpha is .69 and only four alphas are printed for five subscales.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML: Method › Design and Participants, 3rd paragraph; Method › Measures › Stigma and Attribution Assessment, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the sample is less dominated by young adults than 'the majority' suggests, and one subscale's reliability is borderline or unreported.
